title: Mark Python-2.0.1, PSF-2.0, CNRI-Python-GPL-Compatible and CNRI-Python as FSF Free/Libre
body:
The FSF page on licensing covers the different Python licenses.

Both [License of Python 1.6a2 and earlier versions](https://directory.fsf.org/wiki?title=License:Python1.6a2) and [License of Python 2.0.1, 2.1.1, and newer versions](https://directory.fsf.org/wiki?title=License:Python2.0.1) are included in the list of licenses that "qualify as free software licenses, and are compatible with the GNU GPL".
The [License of Python 1.6b1 through 2.0 and 2.1](https://directory.fsf.org/wiki/License:Python1.6b1) is included in the list of licenses that "are free software licenses, but are not compatible with the GNU GPL.

[FSF's entry for Python 2.0.1, 2.1.1](https://directory.fsf.org/wiki/License:Python-2.0.1) identically matches text of `Python-2.0.1` and contains the following licenses with separate SPDX-identifiers: `PSF-2.0`, `CNRI-Python-GPL-Compatible`.

I conclude that `Python-2.0.1`, `PSF-2.0` and `CNRI-Python-GPL-Compatible` are GPL-compatible Free Software licenses.

[FSF's entry for Python 1.6.b1](https://directory.fsf.org/wiki/License:Python-1.6b1) closely matches the text of `CNRI-Python`. It is not exactly the same as FSF lists the license of Python 1.6 (non-beta) and SPDX entry for `NCRI-Python` contains the 1.6-beta-1 version. The key distinction with `CNRI-Python-GPL-Compatible` is article 7 that specifies applicable law. Article 7 is equal between FSF's entry for Python 1.6.b1 and `CNRI-Python`.

I conclude that `CNRI-Python` is a Free Software license that is not GPL-compatible, but it should still get the 'y' in the 'FSF Free/Libre' column.

For completeness, the `Python-2.0` license is already marked OSI-approved and Free Software and contains the license texts of `PSF-2.0` and `CNRI-Python-GPL-Compatible`.

I was triggered to submit this issue by [discussions for choosing the appropriate license identifier for the Argparse NPM package](https://github.com/nodeca/argparse/pull/188).

I couldn't figure out the source of the 'FSF Free/Libre'-column. Perhaps it can be improved in the documentation.

title: New license request: MIT License with Proof-of-Usage Condition (MIT-PoU), v1.2.0
body:
**Third filing, and the settled one.** [#3064](https://github.com/spdx/license-list-XML/issues/3064) was closed when its tag was superseded; [#3065](https://github.com/spdx/license-list-XML/issues/3065) tracked the licence through `v1.1.1` and `v1.2.0` by edits, and its history reads like the drafting it was. This request replaces it, filed clean at **`v1.2.0`** — the version whose wording is settled — with the adoption list current. The prior issue is closed with a pointer here.

### How license meets inclusion principles

Taking the principles in order — the definitive factors first, then the others — including where
this licence does not meet them.

#### Definitive factors

**A. It does not match a licence already on the list.** Checked against the SPDX matching
guidelines and `DOCS/license-match.md`. The permission grant is MIT verbatim, but the licence adds
a substantive condition — roughly forty lines defining a record obligation, a credits obligation
and the hash that ties them together — which no listed licence contains. Its nearest relative in
effect rather than wording is BSD-4-Clause, whose advertising clause is a different obligation in
different words. If the Legal Team reads the matching guidelines as reaching this, I would rather
be told than have a duplicate listed.

**B. Not OSI-approved,** so this factor does not apply. Stated again under factor 1 below.

**C. It is a source licence.** The grant is MIT: source is distributed under it, and the added
condition does not restrict source availability in any way.

**D. The text is identifiable and stable, and is not in the midst of drafting.** Frozen at tag
`v1.2.0`, and that is the text pasted below. The version history, stated rather than left to a
diff: `v1.1.1` changed the heading of `v1.0.1` to carry the short identifier; `v1.2.0` reworded
the record clause to state what the markup notes always intended — the provenance branch name is
a suggestion, any branch that accepts pull requests serves, and absent a designation the default
branch is the designated one. The grant, both halves of the condition and the hash rule are
unchanged since `v1.0`.

**E. The steward commits to stability.** I am the steward, and the text at `v1.2.0` will not be
modified after addition to the list: the tag stays where it points, and no revision of those terms
is published under it or under the identifier `MIT-PoU`. A change to the terms would be a new
version at a new tag, submitted as a separate request with its own identifier, so that anything
already labelled `MIT-PoU` keeps meaning exactly what it means today. Documentation around the
licence may continue to change; the licence file at the tag will not.

#### Other factors

**1. Compliance with an open source definition — it does not, and I am not claiming otherwise.**
The added condition places an obligation on a class of user, which the OSD does not permit. This
falls to be considered under factor 4 instead: the licence is intended for free distribution of
source with limited restrictions. The grant is MIT in full — use, modify, sell, sublicense, no
payment, no revenue share, no field-of-use limit. What it adds is a disclosure obligation on
operators of automated systems: record the use in the repository, and name the work in the credits
of whatever that use produced. If the Legal Team's reading is that factor 1 is definitive and
factor 4 does not reach this, that is a fair outcome and I would rather hear it than have it
listed on a misunderstanding.

**2. Generally usable by anyone.** Yes. It is published as a template with `[Year]` and
`[Copyright Holders]` placeholders, plus tooling (`npx proof-of-usage licence`) and a validation
workflow. It names no project, company or consortium. The provenance branch name and record
filename are given as suggestions in the text itself as of `v1.2.0`. The underlying
record/credit/hash mechanism is additionally specified licence-independently, as the public-domain
[Proof of Usage PoU/1.0](https://github.com/origami-ltd/proof-of-usage), usable beside unmodified
MIT, Apache-2.0 or GPL as a request — this licence is the variant where the request is a
condition, and it is submitted on its own terms rather than as the only way to the mechanism.

**3. Actual, substantial use.** Seven repositories, and I will not dress the number up. Four are
mine — the wasm.ltd game-preservation projects and the licence's own repository. Three are not,
all adopted within four days of publication:

- [mrxenginner/reVC](https://github.com/mrxenginner/reVC) (~257 stars) — the reverse-engineered
  GTA Vice City codebase, whose maintainers had previously declined to attach any licence at all.
  Adopted 13 August 2026 in [reVC#37](https://github.com/mrxenginner/reVC/pull/37).
- [Polyphase-Labs/Polyphase-Engine](https://github.com/Polyphase-Labs/Polyphase-Engine) (~55
  stars) — a game engine, previously unlicensed. Adopted 16 August 2026 in
  [Polyphase-Engine#50](https://github.com/Polyphase-Labs/Polyphase-Engine/pull/50), merged by the
  project's own maintainer account, with its own copyright holder in the notice
  (`Copyright (c) 2022 Martin Holtkamp`) and the register and discovery document both present.
- [gumiranda/cloudfunding](https://github.com/gumiranda/cloudfunding) — adopted 14 August 2026,
  with the caveat that its copyright notice names its author and me jointly.

Disclosed rather than left to be found: I proposed all three as pull requests; the maintainers
reviewed and merged them. That is how a new licence reaches anyone, but a reviewer should hear it
from me. If the answer is still "come back when there is more", that is reasonable and I will.

**4. Free distribution with limited restrictions.** Yes — see 1.

**5. Steward's position.** I am the steward and I am making this request.

**Markup notes for the XML.** `[Year]` and `[Copyright Holders]` are the standard replaceable
copyright fields. As of `v1.2.0` the branch-name flexibility is stated in the clause itself rather
than needing markup. Some adopting repositories append a project-specific appendix *after* the
licence text, naming a service that opens the required pull request for systems that cannot open
one themselves; that is an offer by those projects and not part of these terms, and appended text
should sit outside the identifier for matching purposes.

### Suggested short identifier

### License or Exception?

### URL to license text

https://github.com/origami-ltd/mit-proof-of-usage-license/blob/v1.2.0/LICENSE.md

(Frozen at tag `v1.2.0`. Plain-page rendering of the same text:
https://origami-ltd.github.io/mit-proof-of-usage-license/#text)

- https://github.com/Polyphase-Labs/Polyphase-Engine — adopted 16 Aug 2026, [#50](https://github.com/Polyphase-Labs/Polyphase-Engine/pull/50); not the author's, own copyright holder

title: Correct the EPICS licence text and source reference
body:
The EPICS entry in `src/EPICS.xml` points only to the former `epics.anl.gov` page. The current official EPICS licensing page is:

https://epics-controls.org/licensing/

That page links the LICENSE Text which projects are instructed to copy and customise. It should be added as the current cross-reference; the historical URL can remain in accordance with SPDX policy.

There are also two problems in the recorded text.

Clause 6 currently says:

> DO NOT REPTHAT USE OF THE SOFTWARE WOULD NOT INFRINGE PRIVATELY OWNED RIGHTS

The official text says:

> DO NOT REPRESENT THAT USE OF THE SOFTWARE WOULD NOT INFRINGE PRIVATELY OWNED RIGHTS

The missing `RESENT ` is present in both the licence text and standard template, and consequently in generated outputs.

The SPDX entry also begins with “EPICS Open License Terms” and a paragraph explaining that the following text applies to EPICS Base and support modules. These came from the old ANL webpage and are explanatory page content, not part of the LICENSE Text distributed with EPICS projects. The current licensing instructions distinguish the webpage from the LICENSE Text and tell projects to customise only the words inside chevrons.

Could the current official source be added, `REPTHAT` be corrected to `REPRESENT THAT`, and the old webpage heading and introductory paragraph be removed from the mandatory licence text? If retaining the latter for matching historical copies is useful, they could instead be marked optional.

title: SimPL-2.0: Fix OSI URL and mark last section as optional
body:
The last section of SimPL-2.0 text is not strictly part of the license itself, so this PR marks it as optional, to avoid conveying misleading guidance to users.

Additionally, the OSI URL (modified in PR #2960) has incorrect capitalization: it is written as "SiMPL" instead of "SimPL". Although that URL does work, resolving to the correct page, the capitalization does not match the actual license's short name, and can be potentially misleading, so this PR also corrects the URL.

While modifying the file, I took the opportunity to fix some indentation inconsistencies in this file.

Finally, this PR corrects a punctuation inconsistency in the list of disclaimers: the last item in that list currently ends with a semicolon, which is a leftover from an [earlier draft](https://lists.opensource.org/pipermail/license-discuss_lists.opensource.org/2007-March/012630.html) in which an additional list item followed it. When that extra item was removed, the semicolon in the item before it should have been adjusted to a period, but that detail appears to have been missed at the time. This PR fixes the punctuation to ensure the consistency of the recorded text.

Each of the changes above are made in separate, atomic commits, so that they can be reviewed independently (I would suggest viewing the [diff in whitespace-insensitive mode](https://github.com/spdx/license-list-XML/pull/2988/changes?w=1)), and dropped if undesirable (or split to separate PRs if that's preferred).

❓ It is unknown if the license steward (Amazon AWS) is committed to not modifying the license after addition to the list and to versioning new versions in the future, however the license text doesn't appear to have changed since it was published in 2008.

✅ The license is structured to be generally usable by anyone. It is not specific to one project, consortium or corporation.
❓ The license was used in at least one popular project (a [Java client library for Amazon Kinesis](https://github.com/awslabs/amazon-kinesis-client)), however that project was re-licensed under `Apache-2.0` several years ago.

title: New license request: Archive-packaging-exception [SPDX-Online-Tools]
body:
**1.** License name: Archive Packaging Exception
**2.** Short identifier: Archive-packaging-exception
**3.** License author or steward: ale5000
**4.** Comments: This exception addresses a specific gap in the current SPDX License List regarding the distribution of software in aggregated, compressed, or containerized formats.
While existing exceptions focus on software linking (API/Library), this proposal focuses on the Packaging Process.

Possible uses:

1) System and Platform Modding: In ecosystems such as mobile platforms, custom firmware, and embedded systems, GPLv3-licensed automation scripts must be bundled into installable archives (e.g., flashable ZIPs).
These archives often require the inclusion of independent third-party modules or assets with incompatible licenses. This exception provides a clear legal framework to treat these as "Independent Modules" within the same distribution container.

2) Containerization (Docker and OCI Images): As software moves toward containerized distribution, users often build images where GPLv3 components coexist with proprietary or differently licensed tools.
This exception clarifies that such bundling—where components interact through standard interfaces—does not extend the copyleft requirements to the entire container image.

3) Modern CI/CD and Security Compliance: Modern distribution requires archives to be validated and digitally signed.
This exception explicitly protects the use of digital signing tools, code coverage, and profiling analysis tools within an "Eligible Packaging Process," ensuring that security and quality compliance do not conflict with the license terms.

4) Protection of Copyleft Integrity: A key feature of this exception is the explicit exclusion of derivative works.
It ensures that "Independent Modules" must be truly independent under copyright law. If a module is based on the GPLv3 components, it remains subject to the full GPLv3 requirements, thus preventing any "weakening" of the core copyleft protections.

body:
MPL-2.0 was added back in 2012 and to accommodate the additional option to use MPL's Exhibit B, which effectively negates the copyleft compatibility clause in section 3.3

The id uses the word "exception" - I believe this predates the existence of the `WITH` modifier and the exception list, as we have since then endeavored to NOT include the word "exception" in license ids. 

It has been suggested more recently that this is a bit confusing. Also, Exhibit B would be interpreted as more of a restriction than an exception. 

Changing a license id is not something we do often and must receive much careful consideration, so I'm logging this a s discuss on a legal call.

See https://github.com/spdx/license-list-XML/issues/1637 for some previous commentary on this.

title: Consider differentiating customizable text from simple variation-handling?
body: ## Uses of `` Currently, the `` tag is used in two fundamentally different capacities. ### As a field to mark customizable text Many of the license texts include customizable details related to the project being licensed, like project name, copyright statements, maintainer or rightsholder addresses, etc. These are frequently wrapped in an alt tag that will match anything (`match=".*"`), although a few have more specific matching patterns. A variable name is always specified (name="something") to capture the matched string. For example, in `BSD-2-Clause.xml`, the text specifying "THE COPYRIGHT HOLDER(S) (AND|OR) CONTRIBUTORS" are made customizable in two places, captured as `copyrightHolderAsIs` and `copyrightHolderLiability`: https://github.com/spdx/license-list-XML/blob/9269d7211fba83092697d5211c5f81988222ec84/src/BSD-2-Clause.xml#L30 https://github.com/spdx/license-list-XML/blob/9269d7211fba83092697d5211c5f81988222ec84/src/BSD-2-Clause.xml#L33 In `Python-2.0.1.xml`, the specific Python version for which the license applies is similarly captured in a number of places, using a more specific regular expression: https://github.com/spdx/license-list-XML/blob/9269d7211fba83092697d5211c5f81988222ec84/src/Python-2.0.1.xml#L35 https://github.com/spdx/license-list-XML/blob/9269d7211fba83092697d5211c5f81988222ec84/src/Python-2.0.1.xml#L84 ### To support minor variations in license texts Other uses of alt tags aren't free-form/customizable at all, but merely prevent slight variations in license text from causing a failure to match the license. Going back to `BSD-2-Clause.xml`, the word "EXPRESS" is surrounded by an alt tag not because it's customizable, but simply because some versions of the text contain "EXPRESSED" instead of "EXPRESS": https://github.com/spdx/license-list-XML/blob/9269d7211fba83092697d5211c5f81988222ec84/src/BSD-2-Clause.xml#L31 The same is true in `xpp.xml`, where "University" may be misspelled as "Univeristy", and where a certain conjunction may be either "and" or "or" (but nothing else): https://github.com/spdx/license-list-XML/blob/9269d7211fba83092697d5211c5f81988222ec84/src/xpp.xml#L40 ### Other tags handled as replaceable This also applies to e.g. `` and ``, which are presented identically as red replaceable text, despite having different purposes. It makes sense for a project to customize the copyright text of its license as needed, so `` can fairly be treated like the first category of `` tags above. But the bullets used in the license are more akin to the second type of `` tag above, in that there are a fairly limited set of possibilities for what might be found in their place. The `1.` before the first clause in `BSD-2-Clause.xml` might be replaced with `1)`, or `1 —`, or even nothing if the list is numbered automatically, but it probably shouldn't be replaced with `45)` or `apple)`. ## Presentation of `` Software doesn't care about the purpose of a given `` tag, and for the purposes of matching the information that it's replaceable is sufficient. But to humans, the implications of the two types of "replaceable" text are unlikely to be the same. And because these two very different situations are _handled_ the same way in the code/data, they're also **presented** the same way on the website. All replaceable text is presented in red, so the handling of variations appears to indicate that unexpected bits of text are customizable or free-form, when in fact they're not. In the display of `BSD-2-Clause.xml`, for example, it seems potentially confusing for "EXPRESS" to be shown in the same red text as "THE COPYRIGHT HOLDERS AND CONTRIBUTORS" — at least, without also providing some explanation for why and how someone would "customize" the word EXPRESS: ![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/552e8ce1-7600-4867-8f2b-3f9f757a9c98) Since optional and replaceable texts _are_ indicated to humans by coloring the text blue or red, respectively, it's presumably of some value to highlight those locations. But if "there could be anything here" freely-customizable areas of the text, and other areas where only a very limited set of options will pass, are all presented the same, it seems as though that value could be somewhat reduced?

title: Review Python-* / PSF-* licenses together with OSI page
body:
There are (at least) three different Python-related license IDs on the License List:

* [Python-2.0](https://spdx.org/licenses/Python-2.0.html)
* [Python-2.0.1](https://spdx.org/licenses/Python-2.0.1.html)
* [PSF-2.0](https://spdx.org/licenses/PSF-2.0.html)

Many, many gory details about these different versions are available at https://github.com/spdx/license-list-XML/issues/1200, but the upshot is:

* Python-2.0 was probably never actually used for Python release 2.0, but it's the version that was approved by OSI
* Python-2.0.1 was added to the License List in #1549 as a version of the Python "license stack" which more closely aligns with the version actually used by Python
* PSF-2.0 contains just the first section of the Python "license stack," and is used by others in the Python community separately from distributions of Python itself

I'm mentioning all of this because it appears that OSI still has the text of Python-2.0 on its website at https://opensource.org/license/python-2-0/. However, at some point between May 2023 and now, they updated the corresponding SPDX identifier on the OSI site to be `PSF-2.0` instead of `Python-2.0`. (see the Wayback Machine at http://web.archive.org/web/20230526114956/https://opensource.org/license/python-2-0/ for where this previously said `Python-2.0`)

This means that the text on the OSI site no longer matches the specified identifier on the License List; and the License List's designation of which Python- / PSF- licenses are OSI-approved is no longer in line with what OSI says.

I think there's a couple of options for addressing this:

1. OSI might correct their page back to use the `Python-2.0` identifier
2. or, OSI might change the text on that page to be what SPDX calls `PSF-2.0`, and we can update the identifiers accordingly

@richardfontana @jlovejoy I'd welcome your thoughts on the above!

cc @OpenSourceOrg if you have feedback as well!

title: W3C appears to refer to the wrong license for OSI approval
body:
Hi, I think I found a discrepancy in the W3C license references. There are three variants tracked in the license list: [W3C](https://spdx.org/licenses/W3C.html), [W3C-19980720](https://spdx.org/licenses/W3C-19980720.html), and [W3C-20150513](https://spdx.org/licenses/W3C-20150513.html).

[W3C](https://spdx.org/licenses/W3C.html) is marked as OSI-approved, but the license text differs from [OSI's static copy](https://opensource.org/license/w3c-php/). The OSI static copy instead matches [W3C-19980720](https://spdx.org/licenses/W3C-19980720.html), despite the fact that OSI's site references the SPDX identifier for the 2015 version.

Based upon OSI's page, it looks like they either approved the 1998 or 2015 version, which means [W3C](https://spdx.org/licenses/W3C.html) probably shouldn't be marked as OSI approved. Again, purely based upon [the text](https://opensource.org/license/w3c-php/), the OSI approved flag should likely go with [W3C-19980720](https://spdx.org/licenses/W3C-19980720.html).

title: Consider changes to Unicode-TOU
body:
This is following from the discussion on the spdx-legal mailing list at https://lists.spdx.org/g/Spdx-legal/topic/97116566

[`Unicode-TOU`](https://spdx.org/licenses/Unicode-TOU.html) is not a versioned identifier. It points to the license text for the Unicode Terms of Use as they existed as of (I believe) 2014. But the terms of use posted on the Unicode website at https://www.unicode.org/copyright.html have evolved over time, and the mailing list thread discusses how this has caused some confusion with folks using `Unicode-TOU` to refer to the wrong set of terms.

A separate issue #1851 discusses whether to add a new, separate identifier with the current updated terms.

For the current `Unicode-TOU` identifier, we should consider either or both of the following options:
1. For the license's `Full name`, modify it to be `Unicode Terms of Use - 2014` or something similar, to help emphasize that it is the 2014 version (again, assuming that's the correct year - should be verified); and/or
2. Deprecate `Unicode-TOU` as an identifier, and add a new ID `Unicode-TOU-2014` with the same existing content.

I'm in favor of 1, and on the fence for 2. Interested in other community members' thoughts.

For clarity, in neither case would we remove `Unicode-TOU` as a valid identifier. It would remain valid (even if deprecated) and pointing to the existing license text that's currently associated with it.
